ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Endocrinology Consultation — Swami Vivekananda — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Diagnosis visit with the endocrinology consultation: A1c, fasting glucose, GAD antibodies, C-peptide, urine albumin, lipids and B12; type 2 diabetes confirmed; metformin by shared decision; nutrition and fasting plans

text.paragraph: Two months of thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and about 4 kg weight loss in a 35-year-old Hindu monk of South Asian ancestry with a BMI of 24.7 and a random glucose of 246 mg/dL, told of diabetes a year ago and never tested or treated except by diet. Please confirm and classify the diabetes with the fasting tests drawn on the morning of your visit, and advise on treatment that fits his mostly vegetarian monastic diet, his religious fasts and his frequent travel. [S]

list.item: Is this type 2 diabetes, or type 1, slowly progressive autoimmune or another type, and which tests decide it?
With symptoms and weight loss, does he need insulin now, or can he start with tablets?
Which medicines best fit his religious fasts, his mostly vegetarian diet and long periods of travel?
How should he keep his fasts safely, and when should he break a fast?
How should the kidneys be protected, given any albuminuria and his raised blood pressure?
What targets and monitoring do you advise, including lipids at 35 with South Asian ancestry?

text.paragraph: Swami Vivekananda, 35, a Hindu monk, is seen at the request of Dr. Thornbury-Mensah for two months of thirst, nocturia, tiredness and weight loss. He was told of diabetes a year ago and has managed it only by diet. He eats mostly vegetarian meals at his monastery, with fish at some, and keeps fasts twice a month and at major festivals; a few days ago a night-long waterless fast left him light-headed and very thirsty. He calls diabetes hereditary in his family. He prefers tablets to injections but will accept what is needed. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: He was born Narendranath (Narendra Nath) Datta in an affluent family in Calcutta (Kolkata) on 12 January 1863. His father, Vishwanath Datta, was a successful attorney; his mother was Bhuvaneshwari Devi. [D]
He met Sri Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar in November 1881 and became his disciple; in 1887 he and his brother disciples took the formal vows of sannyasa and new monastic names. [D]

He left Bombay for America on 31 May 1893 and spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in September 1893, which made him famous; he then spent nearly three and a half years teaching Vedanta, mostly in the eastern United States and London, and returned to India in January 1897. [D]

On 1 May 1897, at a meeting of the monastic and lay devotees of Sri Ramakrishna in Calcutta, he founded the Ramakrishna Mission Association; in February 1898 the monastery moved to a garden house at Belur on the west bank of the Ganga, and land for the Belur Math was bought in early 1898. [D]

In March and April 1897, soon after his return to India, he wrote that he had diabetes. On 16 March he wrote: "The work has broken me down completely, and I have got 'diabetes', an incurable disease"; on 26 March: "The result of this steady work in the West and the tremendous work of a month in India upon the Bengalee constitution is 'diabetes'. It is a hereditary foe," adding that "Eating only meat and drinking no water seems to be the only way to prolong life"; and on 7 April that he had been "attacked by 'Diabetes', a fell disease" and had gone to Darjeeling, cool and "very good for the disease," where the doctors did not want him to move about. A biography says he went to Darjeeling on the advice of physicians. [D]

On 29 May 1897, from Almora, he wrote to a physician disciple that he was taking the medicines sent to him, riding morning and evening and feeling very strong, but that "I never in my life could sleep as soon as I got into bed. I must toss for at least two hours," that he felt hot after the evening meal, that "There has not been any thirst even though the days are fearfully hot," and that he was afraid of "getting fat on a too much milk diet." [D]

Diabetes to be confirmed and classified (type 2, type 1 or slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes) with A1c, fasting glucose, GAD antibodies and C-peptide

list.item: Type 2 diabetes (E11.65). Question 1: diabetes is confirmed by two abnormal results (A1c 9.4 percent, fasting glucose 172 mg/dL). GAD65 antibodies are negative and his fasting C-peptide is preserved, so this is type 2 diabetes; slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes is unlikely, though antibodies should be rechecked if he loses weight again or needs rapidly escalating treatment. Monogenic diabetes is unlikely without a clear three-generation pattern. In South Asians type 2 diabetes appears earlier and at lower BMI, with more insulin resistance for a given weight, which is why ADA screens Asian Americans from a BMI of 23. Question 2: insulin is not needed now. He has no ketosis, his own insulin secretion is good and the A1c is below 10 percent; his weight loss reflects glucose spilling into the urine and should stop with treatment. [S]

Moderately increased albuminuria, first sample (R80.9). Question 5: 46 mg/g on one sample, which hyperglycemia can raise; it needs two of three abnormal samples over three to six months before diabetic kidney disease is diagnosed. [S]
Raised blood pressure (R03.0). Clinic and home readings of about 136/86: with diabetes and albuminuria the target is below 130/80. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Thornbury-Mensah's intake note: random glucose 246 mg/dL; urine glucose 3+ without ketones; creatinine 0.96, eGFR 106; BMI 24.7; blood pressure 138/86. This morning, fasting: A1c 9.4 percent; plasma glucose 172 mg/dL; GAD65 antibodies 1.2 IU/mL (negative); C-peptide 2.6 ng/mL; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 46 mg/g; total cholesterol 214, HDL 36, triglycerides 228, LDL 132 mg/dL; ALT 38 U/L (FIB-4 0.6); TSH 1.8; vitamin B12 312 pg/mL. Home blood pressure average 136/86. [S]

list.item: Question 3: start metformin extended-release with the evening meal, 500 mg for a week, then 1000 mg, rising to 1872 mg if tolerated; extended-release taken with the meal that ends a fast suits his fasts. A second tablet now would also be reasonable at this A1c, but starting with metformin and diet and reviewing in about five weeks is safe and is his preference. Avoid sulfonylureas, which cause hypoglycemia during fasts. A GLP-1 receptor agonist is not the first choice for a man who has just lost weight unintentionally and prefers tablets. [S]
Once albuminuria is confirmed, add an SGLT2 inhibitor for kidney and heart protection, with clear rules: skip it on waterless fast days and stop it when unable to eat or drink. [S]

Question 4: by IDF-DAR risk stratification, adapted from Ramadan to his fasts, his risk is moderate while glucose is high and low on metformin once it is steady. Fasts with fruit, milk and water are reasonable now; avoid waterless fasts until glucose is steady below 180 mg/dL, and then keep them short and drink well before and after; check glucose at midday and before breaking a fast; break it if glucose is below 70 or above 300 mg/dL, or if he is dizzy, confused or vomiting. [S]

Medical nutrition therapy with a dietitian: a mostly vegetarian plan built on his monastery meals (dal, vegetables, whole grains and yogurt, with smaller portions of rice and sweets), respecting his choices; healthy plant-based diets are associated with better cardiometabolic risk in South Asians. [S]

Question 5: if home blood pressure stays at or above 130/80, an ARB (losartan) rather than an ACE inhibitor; potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after starting; repeat the urine albumin twice over three to six months. [S]

Question 6: A1c target below 7 percent, A1c every three months until at target; retinal photographs and a foot examination at diagnosis; vitamin B12 periodically on metformin; a moderate-intensity statin is reasonable at 35 with diabetes, South Asian ancestry, albuminuria and raised blood pressure; hepatitis B and pneumococcal vaccines. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Thornbury-Mensah the same day. The results and the reasons for each recommendation were explained to Swami Vivekananda, including why his fasts and his diet are his to decide and how the plan adapts to them. He decides who else receives this note. [S]

Follow-up: Endocrinology review in three months, or sooner if glucose stays above 250 mg/dL, ketones appear or he loses weight again; Dr. Thornbury-Mensah continues primary care and shares the monitoring. [S]
